prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Right, When, They

outputs.L1:
I tell my attendants, “Right there,”  
when they rub me where it itches.  
They rub for a few seconds, then move on.  
There’s so much of it to wash—  
“it” being me, a former person,  
now something that must be washed every day  
in so little time.

Fifty minutes outside my breathing machine,  
and all I can do is stare  
as my breath recedes like the woman  
who would not love me.

“It’s almost over,” I say to myself,  
over and over,  
as soon as the machine is turned off.  
An idiotic mantra, perhaps,  
but it helps when the ache descends into my eyes  
and my words quit coming out right.

“Left hand,” I say.

“Right foot?” the attendant asks, guessing.

I begin to fantasize about gusts of air  
rushing down my windpipe with hurricane force.  
Garish and impossible,  
they’re respiratory porn.

My re-entry is stalled  
by the attendant straightening a sheet  
that no one will see.  
Enraged, I squeeze my eyes closed.

“Christ.”

“What?”

“Never mind.”

Once back in and turned on,  
I cough violently and with conviction.  
Shocked by the force of the inrushing air,  
I feel my lungs expand like birthday balloons.  
My terror-flattened mind pops up into 3-D  
as I return to the land of breathing.

*January 1990*
outputs.L2:
I direct my caregivers to the exact spot  
when their hands reach an itch.  
They linger only briefly before continuing—  
there is an entire body to clean.  
That body is mine: once a person,  
now a thing requiring a daily washing  
completed against the clock.

I can survive only fifty minutes  
away from the machine that breathes for me,  
and during that time I can merely watch  
as my air ebbs away, like the woman  
who refused to return my love.

The instant the ventilator is switched off,  
I repeatedly reassure myself:  
Soon this will be finished.  
Perhaps it is a foolish refrain,  
but it steadies me when pain settles behind my eyes  
and speech begins to fail.

“My left hand,” I manage.

“Your right foot?” the caregiver asks, trying to interpret me.

I imagine enormous blasts of air  
tearing through my windpipe like a hurricane.  
The fantasy is lurid, unattainable—  
a kind of pornography for the lungs.

My return to the ventilator is postponed  
while the caregiver smooths a bedsheet  
that nobody will ever notice.  
Furious, I clamp my eyelids shut.

“Christ.”

“What did you say?”

“Forget it.”

At last I am reconnected, and the machine starts.  
I cough with fierce, violent certainty.  
The sudden surge of air astonishes me;  
my lungs swell like balloons at a birthday party.  
My mind, crushed flat by fear,  
rises again into three dimensions  
as I cross back into the world where breathing is possible.

January 1990
outputs.L3:
The speaker relies entirely on attendants to wash and care for his immobilized body, all while working within severe time constraints. He can remain outside his breathing machine for only fifty minutes, and during that brief interval he feels his ability to breathe steadily weakening. As his breath fades, physical pain intensifies and his speech becomes increasingly impaired, making it difficult to communicate even his most urgent needs.

In his desperation, he imagines powerful gusts of air filling his lungs. Any delay in reconnecting the breathing machine provokes both terror and rage, since each passing moment brings him closer to suffocation. Once the machine is finally restored, however, the sudden rush of air revives not only his lungs but also his mind, carrying him back into what he calls the “land of breathing.”
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the daily washing of a ventilator-dependent person as an experience of fear, exposure, and near-total powerlessness. What may appear to the caregivers as an ordinary hygienic routine becomes, for the speaker, a terrifying interruption of the machinery that sustains life. The body is handled quickly and impersonally, reduced to its physical needs and treated almost as an object to be cleaned. Stark bodily imagery emphasizes vulnerability: the speaker cannot move freely, control the pace of the procedure, or communicate distress with ease. Every action performed by others carries the possibility of pain, suffocation, or death.

The poem’s fragmented dialogue intensifies this atmosphere. Brief instructions and hurried exchanges suggest that the caregivers are focused on completing the task rather than recognizing the speaker as a conscious human being. Language becomes another sign of the unequal relationship between them. Those attending the body can speak, decide, and act, while the ventilator-dependent person is largely unable to intervene. Even if the caregivers do not intend cruelty, their efficiency feels dehumanizing because the speaker’s terror remains unseen or unacknowledged.

Against this harsh external reality, the speaker retreats into an internal fantasy. Imagination offers a temporary refuge from physical confinement and from the humiliating loss of control. The contrast between the freedom of the mind and the helplessness of the body makes the situation even more painful. Internally, the speaker remains fully aware, emotionally complex, and capable of desire; externally, others may perceive only a passive body attached to medical equipment. The poem therefore challenges any assumption that severe physical dependence diminishes a person’s inner life or humanity.

The return to the ventilator is described not as a gentle comfort but as a forceful, almost violent restoration. Air enters the body with overwhelming intensity, yet that violence is also salvation. The machine is both a symbol of dependence and the means by which life continues. This paradox lies at the center of the poem: the speaker is imprisoned by bodily fragility and medical necessity, but each mechanical breath also affirms survival.

Ultimately, the poem transforms breathing—an act most people perform without thought—into something urgent, precarious, and deeply meaningful. By placing the reader inside the perspective of someone who cannot take breath for granted, it exposes the terror that can accompany dependence on others while insisting on the speaker’s full personhood. The final sense of relief does not erase the indignity of the washing or the fear of disconnection. Instead, it reveals the profound dignity contained in the simple continuation of life: to breathe, even with the help of a machine, is to remain present, conscious, and human.
outputs.L5:
**Right When They Needed It**

They had almost given up. The road was dark, the rain was heavy, and every direction seemed wrong. But right when they needed hope most, a small light appeared in the distance. It did not solve every problem, but it reminded them to keep moving.

Sometimes, the right moment is not when everything becomes easy. It is when people discover they are stronger than they thought—and that they do not have to continue alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem from the perspective of a person dependent on an iron lung, describing the terror of being removed from the breathing machine while attendants bathe them.
counterfactuals.output:
They open the iron weather  
that has held me all night—

unfasten the collar,  
lift my head into the terrible latitude  
of ordinary air.

The machine exhales without me,  
a great animal  
still breathing in the room.

Hands gather beneath my shoulders.  
Someone says, *Ready?*  
as if readiness were a door  
I could choose to walk through.

Then I am out.

My chest forgets its tide.  
The ceiling leaps closer.  
Every second grows teeth.

Warm water touches my skin—  
a cloth across the ribs,  
soap at the hollow of my throat—  
small kindnesses  
performed at the edge of drowning.

They speak softly  
about the basin, the towel,  
the morning beyond the window,

while I count what cannot be counted:

not breaths,  
but their absence;

not time,  
but the widening space  
between me  
and the next mechanical mercy.

Hurry, I beg without sound.  
Hurry.

My body is a locked room  
and panic runs wall to wall,  
striking every surface.

Then metal beneath me,  
the collar closing,  
the seal made sure—

and the lung begins again,

pulling the world into me,  
pushing death back  
one measured inch.

Around us, the bathwater cools.

Someone smooths my hair  
and says, *There.*

As if I have returned  
from nowhere.

As if nowhere  
had not opened its mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a raw first-person disability poem about losing autonomy, struggling to communicate with caregivers, and experiencing overwhelming relief when a ventilator is switched back on. End with “January, 1990.”
counterfactuals.output:
They call it care  
when hands I did not ask for  
roll me, wash me, lift me  
like an object with a pulse.

I try to tell them  
the mask is wrong,  
the angle hurts,  
there is panic gathering  
behind my ribs—

but my mouth is a locked room.  
My tongue drags.  
My breath breaks each word  
before it can become mine.

They say, “Relax.”  
They say, “We know.”  
They speak across my body  
as if I have already left it.

Then the ventilator stops.

The room keeps moving.  
Someone folds a sheet.  
Someone checks a number.  
I am drowning in plain sight,  
screaming without sound,  
every cell begging  
for the machine  
I once hated  
because it owned the rhythm  
of my life.

Switch it on.  
Please.  
Please understand this one thing.

Then—

the motor wakes,  
air rushes into me,  
cold, mechanical, absolute.

My chest rises.

Again.

Again.

I have never loved  
anything so fiercely  
as that stolen breath  
returned.

January, 1990.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, intimate monologue in poetic form in which a formerly independent person compares air rushing into their lungs to “respiratory porn” and their lungs to birthday balloons.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to open every door myself,  
carry my own name like a lit match  
through the long corridors of night.

Now someone lifts the mask to my face,  
and air rushes in—  
shameless, mechanical, necessary—  
respiratory porn,  
the obscene intimacy of being kept alive.

My lungs, once quiet animals,  
are birthday balloons in чужие hands—  
filled, emptied, filled again,  
as if each breath were a celebration  
no one had the courage to cancel.

I listen to the machine  
whisper its cold vows.

I hate how tender it is.  
I hate that I wait for it.

Once, I belonged only to myself.  
Now even the dark must enter me  
by permission.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an unpolished, emotionally intense free-verse poem narrated by a ventilator user during a rushed daily bath, incorporating fragmented dialogue, fear of suffocation, anger at an attendant’s delay, and the sensation of returning to “the land of breathing.”
counterfactuals.output:
“Quick,” I say,  
or try to—  
the word chopped small  
behind the machine’s breath.

“Just a minute.”

No.  
No minute.  
A minute is a country  
you can die in.

The hose lies loose,  
a pale snake across the towel.  
Water runs too hot  
over my ribs,  
soap in the hollow of my throat,  
hands hurrying everywhere  
except where I need them.

“Wait—hold on—”

I am holding.  
I am always holding  
what everyone else gets to spill  
without thinking.

My chest bangs  
against its locked door.

Where are you?  
Where are you?  
Where—

The attendant turns for the washcloth,  
the drawer,  
the stupid clean shirt,  
some small useless thing  
while the room narrows  
to tile  
to steam  
to the black pinhead  
at the center of my sight.

“I’m coming.”

You were supposed to be here.

Anger rises before air does—  
hotter than the water,  
uglier than fear.

I want to throw the basin.  
I want to scream  
with lungs that can afford screaming.

Instead:  
eyes wide,  
fingers clawing once  
at the wet sheet.

Then the tube.  
The connection.  
The click.

The machine catches me  
like a fist in my shirt.

One breath.  
Metallic, enormous.

Another.

My body opens badly,  
painfully,  
like a rusted gate.

“You okay?”

No.

Yes.

Don’t ask me that.

The walls return.  
The towel.  
The half-washed skin.  
Your apologizing mouth.

I cross back shaking  
into the land of breathing,

that brutal green country  
where air enters  
and enters  
and nobody understands  
why I am furious  
to be alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
